newsitem.title: USA: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD/Wall Street sees Fed rate hike.
newsitem.headline: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD/Wall Street sees Fed rate hike.

text.p: Wall Street has seen the future and it's an interest rate increase by the Federal Reserve.
The stock market was on pins and needles this week as investors hardened their focus on a looming interest rate rise by the Fed -- the first in more than two years.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan raised the odds of a monetary tightening, putting investors and consumers on notice that the cost of borrowing could be more expensive, as early as next week.

Greenspan said the central bank, whose job is to be on guard against excesses in the economy, needed to look ahead to price pressures, and he saw underlying inflation this year as the unemployment rate shrinks and the labor market tightens.
Economists are worried that as workers unite, they will be able to demand higher wages after six straight years of economic growth, and that could force companies to boost prices.
But the prospect of tighter monetary policy was disturbing to Wall Street, which has become accustomed to a glorious unchanging future of ever higher stock prices during the last two years.

The rate-hike threat drew a gasping reaction, prompting a sell-off this week that wiped out 130.67 points from the Dow Jones Industrial Average. On Friday, the world's most closely watched index of 30 blue chip stocks ended off 15.49 points at 6,804.79.
Investors have enjoyed the longest running bull market in history, basking in an ideal climate of steady economic growth, tame inflation and low interest rates.

The fear now is that higher interest rates could lead to an unholy scenario. As the cost of borrowing to finance houses and credit card loans rises, it could put a damper on the economy, slowing corporate earnings, which eventually would hurt the stock market.
Financial markets take Greenspan's words seriously because he has the power as central bank boss to make his words come true.
In fact, investors have been looking over their shoulders since December when Greenspan first made his now-famous comment about the markets' irrational exuberance.

He repeated the warnings in February and again this month in more blunt terms, and this week Greenspan appeared to be setting the stage for an increase in interest rates next week, stressing the importance of prompt action to keep inflation down before it hurts the economy.
The Fed could move when policy-makers meet Tuesday.
The latest economic reports strengthened the argument for a pre-emptive move by the Fed to slow economic growth and head off inflationary pressures.
The Commerce Department reported this week that builders broke ground on new homes and apartments in February at the fastest clip in nearly three years.
Total housing starts shot up 12.2 percent to an annual rate of 1.53 million -- the strongest building pace since 1.56 million in March 1994 -- versus a revised 0.7 percent gain in January.

"Federal Reserve Chairman Greenspan wants to move pre-emptively because he does not want to lose his economic victories of the past few years, which have been hard-earned gains," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp.
He said Greenspan's jawboning in the last couple of months may have accomplished some of central bank's goals, which are to deflate the speculation in stocks and boost long-term interest rates.

The Treasury's benchmark 30-year bond jumped this week to the seven percent level for the first time since last September, and the Dow Jones industrial average is now some 290 points below its record high of 7,085.16 set on March 11.

"Greenspan may have all that he needs already but even if the central bank does not raise interest rates in March, then it will need to raise them in May if we see more upward pressure on wages," Johnson said.
Analysts said that by raising interest rates, the Fed would cap the stock market's ascent, which has boosted corporate wealth and spurred job growth and aggravated the tight jobs market.
Faced with a rate hike, the experts are trying to anticipate Wall Street's reaction.

"An interest rate increase by the Federal Reserve would send a message to the stock market to slow things down but it might have a more important effect on market psychology," said Dimitri Papadimitriou, executive director of the Jerome Levy Economics Institute.
He said investors have been "conditioned" to expect a major stock market correction for some time and some have been looking for a good reason to sell stocks.
"An interest rate increase will not kill the stock market but it would sober investors who've been partying it up for the last two years," said George Nickas, a trader at Saul Stone & Co.

"The market has had a very good run and like any other contest there is a beginning and there is an end and Greenspan is just putting out the yellow caution flag telling people to use diligence," he said.
The stock market's problems may not end with an interest rate hike next week.

"The next worry is whether there will be more increases," Johnson said. "Most people realize that the Fed usually doesn't tighten once and it usually ends up raising a number of times. That is clearly the big worry."
